title: Recognize the Team or the Individual Contributors?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article asks whether leaders should publicly recognize the team or individual contributors and concludes that in group settings the team always comes first. It acknowledges that both forms of recognition motivate, but warns that singling out one person for what colleagues see as a team effort breeds jealousy and ill will and can damage collaboration. Individual credit, even when sizeable, is best given in private. When one person's outsized impact must be acknowledged publicly, the leader should name the team first and the contributor second, a small choice the author calls hugely symbolic. The closing argument is that attributing success to the collective builds the spirit teams need, and even top performers know no great achievement is the work of one person.
points: Public elevation of one contributor over the group can create jealousy and erode collaboration, even when the leader means well.
Individual recognition belongs in private settings, while public recognition should credit the collective.
If an individual must be singled out publicly, sequence matters: highlight the team first and the contributor second.
Top performers themselves understand that great achievements are never done by one person, so team-first credit does not cost leaders their stars.
quotes: In group settings, leaders walk a tightrope whenever they elevate individual performance over the team’s collective accomplishment. Attributing team success publicly to any one team member has the potential to create jealousy and ill will within the team. Those who have worked selflessly to support the team take it as a huge insult when leaders single out a particular team member for what they see as a team effort.

Leaders who step unintentionally into this quagmire often learn later that the team is upset and no longer working as collaboratively as they had been prior to this public recognition. Despite the good intentions of leaders to make individuals feel great about their work, in public settings, the team always comes first.

Recognizing team members for their individual contribution, even when it is sizeable, is best left to private settings. The best leaders learn that in a highly collaborative and team-oriented enterprise, just about everything about great performance is attributable to the team, not to individual players.

When one team member has had an oversized impact on the outcome and must be singled out, savvy leaders remember to highlight the team first and the contributor second. On the face of it, this seems like a small and innocuous choice, but it is hugely symbolic.

Leaders who want great teams always recognize the team first and make every attribution of success to the collective. Doing so benefits the spirit and comradery necessary for teams to rally the best effort from everyone.

Leaders help by keeping the pecking order in mind. Turning to individuals after the team has been exalted makes everyone feel good. Even the top performers know that great achievements are never done by one person.
